titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Tuesday, 10 January 1922
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Miss Weaver: Many thanks for the draft received. These few lines are to beg you to send a copy of
The Observer
(marked) also to:
Mr Alessandro Francini
Associazione della Stampa della Venezia Giulia
Piazza Verdi 1,
Trieste (Italy)
He is writing an article for some Italian review.

I have seen a very curious article by Mr Hone in the current number of the London Mercury. Copies of it, I think, ought to be sent also to the three addresses I gave you and to the fourth above – but they would come better from my publisher than from me direct.

Mr Hone’s article is, so far as I know, the first allusion made to me or my writing by any member or hanger-on of the Irish literary movement in an account (in review or paper or history) of that phenomenon. He is, or was, the financer and the head of the firm Maunsel and Co who were responsible for the burning of my book Dubliners . When reading it please pay attention to the last paragraph about which I shall have more to say later on.
By all means send me proofs of Exiles . I shall send you tomorrow more proofs of Ulysses and a photograph which was made for an article to be published in Vanity Fair, New York.

closer.salute: With very many thanks from your troublesome petitioner and his kindest regards

div.note: “Ulysses: James Joyce and his chef d’oeuvre”, The Observer (11 December 1921): 9.

See Alessandro Francini Bruni’s Joyce intimo spogliato in piazza (un’indiavolata caricatura dello scrittore irlandese), Trieste: La Editoriale Libraria, 1922. An English translation was published in James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 14, no. 2 (Winter 1977): 127-59.

This article is J. M. Hone’s “A Letter from Ireland” published in London Mercury, 5, no. 27 (January 1922): 306-08. The last paragraph begins, “For us in Ireland Mr. Joyce’s significance lies in this, that he is the first man of literary genius, expressing himself in perfect freedom, that Catholic Ireland has produced in modern times”.
On 11 September 1912 printer John Falconer burned 1,000 copies of Dubliners before its anticipated publication by Maunsel & Co. See JJ to Pound, 10 March 1916, note 7.
See Djuna Barnes’s “A Portrait of the Man Who Is, at Present, One of the More Significant Figures in Literature” published in Vanity Fair, vol. 18, no. 2 (April 1922): 65, 104.
